stem: What is the solid angle subtended by the moon at any point of the Earth, given the diameter of the moon is 3474 km and its distance from the Earth \(3.84 \times 10^{8}\) m.
solution:
Solid angle subtended by the moon at the Earth
\(= \dfrac{\text{Area of the disc of the moon}}{(\text{moon - earth distance})^{2}}\)
\(= \dfrac{\pi \times (1.737 \times 10^{3})^{2}}{(3.84 \times 10^{5})^{2}}\)
\(= 6.425 \times 10^{-5}\) sr
_note: The stem gives the moon-earth distance in metres (\(3.84 \times 10^{8}\) m) while the printed working substitutes \(3.84 \times 10^{5}\) and the moon's radius as \(1.737 \times 10^{3}\) - i.e. it silently works in kilometres. The ratio, and therefore the answer, is unaffected. Transcribed as printed.

stem: A star is 5.5 light years away from the Earth. How much parallax in arcsec will it subtend when viewed from two opposite points along the orbit of the Earth?
solution:
Two opposite points A and B along the orbit of the Earth are 2 AU apart. The angle subtended by AB at the position of the star is \(=\) AB/distance of the star from the Earth
\(= \dfrac{2\,\text{AU}}{5.5\,l\text{y}} = \dfrac{2 \times 1.496 \times 10^{11}\,\text{m}}{5.5 \times 9.46 \times 10^{15}\,\text{m}} = 5.75 \times 10^{-6}\) rad
\(= 5.75 \times 10^{-6} \times 57.297 \times 60 \times 60\) arcsec
\(= 1.186\) arcsec
_note: The chapter's own 'Do you know' box on the facing page states 1 light year \(= 9.467 \times 10^{15}\) m, while this printed solution substitutes \(9.46 \times 10^{15}\) m. The two differ in the third significant figure; the quoted 3-significant-figure answer 1.186 arcsec is unchanged either way. Transcribed as printed.

stem: The moon is at a distance of \(3.84 \times 10^{8}\) m from the Earth. If viewed from two diametrically opposite points on the Earth, the angle subtended at the moon is \(1^{\circ}\,54'\). What is the diameter of the Earth?
solution:
Angle subtended
\(\theta = 1^{\circ}\,54' = 114' = 114 \times 2.91 \times 10^{-4}\) rad
\(= 3.317 \times 10^{-2}\) rad
Diameter of the Earth \(= \theta \times\) distance to the moon from the Earth
\(= 3.317 \times 10^{-2} \times 3.84 \times 10^{8}\) m
\(= 1.274 \times 10^{7}\) m

stem: A calorie is a unit of heat and it equals 4.2 J, where 1 J \(=\) kg m\(^{2}\) s\(^{-2}\). A distant civilisation employs a system of units in which the units of mass, length and time are \(\alpha\) kg, \(\beta\) m and \(\gamma\) s. Also \(\mathrm{J}'\) is their unit of energy. What will be the magnitude of calorie in their units?
solution:
Let us write the new units as A, B and C for mass, length and time respectively. We are given
\(1\,\mathrm{A} = \alpha\) kg
\(1\,\mathrm{B} = \beta\) m
\(1\,\mathrm{C} = \gamma\) s
\(1\) cal \(= 4.2\) J \(= 4.2\) kg m\(^{2}\) s\(^{-2}\)
\(= 4.2 \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{\alpha} \right) \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\beta} \right)^{2} \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{C}}{\gamma} \right)^{-2}\)
\(= \dfrac{4.2\,\gamma^{2}}{\alpha \beta^{2}}\ \mathrm{A}\mathrm{B}^{2}\mathrm{C}^{-2}\)
\(= \dfrac{4.2\,\gamma^{2}}{\alpha \beta^{2}}\ \mathrm{J}'\)
Thus in the new units, 1 calorie is \(= \dfrac{4.2\,\gamma^{2}}{\alpha \beta^{2}}\ \mathrm{J}'\)

stem: The radius of a sphere measured repeatedly yields values 5.63 m, 5.54 m, 5.44 m, 5.40 m and 5.35 m. Determine the most probable value of radius and the mean absolute, relative and percentage errors.
_note: Significant-figures observation, NOT asserted as a book defect: the five readings are each given to 2 decimal places, yet the mean is printed to 3 decimal places (5.472 m) and the mean absolute error to 4 (0.0904 m), both more precise than any input. The relative error (0.017) and percentage error (1.7%) are, by contrast, correctly rounded to 2 significant figures, so the example is internally inconsistent about precision. Section 1.9 of this chapter states rules for DETERMINING significant figures and for order of magnitude but prints NO rule for rounding the result of an arithmetic operation, so there is no stated rule for this to contradict. Arithmetic verified correct throughout (sum 27.36, mean 5.472; deviations 0.158, 0.068, 0.032, 0.072, 0.122 summing to 0.452). Transcribed as printed.

stem: In an experiment to determine the volume of an object, mass and density are recorded as \(m = (5 \pm 0.15)\) kg and \(\rho = (5 \pm 0.2)\) kg m\(^{-3}\) respectively. Calculate percentage error in the measurement of volume.
solution:
We know,
Density \(= \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}}\)
\(\therefore\) Volume \(= \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Density}} = \dfrac{M}{\rho}\)
Maximum percentage error in volume
\(= \left( \dfrac{\Delta m}{m} + \dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \right) \times 100\)
\(= \left( \dfrac{0.15}{5} + \dfrac{0.2}{5} \right) \times 100\)
\(= (0.03 + 0.04) \times 100\)
\(= (0.07) \times 100 = 7\%\)

stem: The acceleration due to gravity is determined by using a simple pendulum of length \(l = (100 \pm 0.1)\) cm. If its time period is \(T = (2 \pm 0.01)\) s, find the maximum percentage error in the measurement of \(g\).
solution:
The time period of oscillation of a simple pendulum is given by
\(T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}\)
Squaring both sides
\(T^{2} = 4\pi^{2} l / g\)
\(\therefore g = 4\pi^{2} \dfrac{l}{T^{2}}\)
Now \(\Delta l = 0.1,\ l = 100\) cm, \(\Delta T = 0.01\) s, \(T = 2\) s
Maximum Percentage error \(= \dfrac{\Delta g \times 100}{g}\)
\(= \left( \dfrac{\Delta l}{l} + \dfrac{2 \Delta T}{T} \right) \times 100\)
\(= \left( \dfrac{0.1}{100} + \dfrac{2 \times 0.01}{2} \right) \times 100\)
\(= (0.001 + 0.01) \times 100 = 1.1\)
Maximum percentage error in measurement of \(g\) is \(1.1\%\)

stem: The distance travelled by an object in time \((100 \pm 1)\) s is \((5.2 \pm 0.1)\) m. What is the speed and it's relative error?
_note: Book defect in the printed answer: a RELATIVE error is a ratio and is dimensionless, but the key attaches the unit m s^-1 to it. The number is right (0.1/5.2 + 1/100 = 0.0292); the unit is spurious. The absolute error would be 0.0292 x 0.052 = 0.0015 m s^-1, which is not the printed figure, so 0.0292 is definitely the relative error. The same defect recurs in Ex Q.3 (viii), where a relative error is printed in ohms.

stem: A large ball 2 m in radius is made up of a rope of square cross section with edge length 4 mm. Neglecting the air gaps in the ball, what is the total length of the rope to the nearest order of magnitude?

Nuclear radius \(R\) has a dependence on the mass number \((A)\) as \(R = 1.3 \times 10^{-16} A^{1/3}\) m. For a nucleus of mass number \(A = 125\), obtain the order of magnitude of \(R\) expressed in metre.
_note: Two things worth recording, neither of which is an error in the printed answer. (1) The printed answer -15 follows only from this chapter's OWN order-of-magnitude convention, stated in section 1.9 as A x 10^n with 0.5 <= A < 5: R = 6.5 x 10^-16 m is rewritten as 0.65 x 10^-15, giving order -15. Under the conventional 1 <= A < 10 the answer would be -16. (2) The stem's constant 1.3 x 10^-16 m is an order of magnitude smaller than the accepted nuclear radius parameter (about 1.2-1.3 x 10^-15 m, i.e. 1.3 fm). Transcribed as printed; the printed answer is consistent with the printed stem.

_note: Typesetting defect in the printed answer, verified at 4x magnification: every ZERO exponent in this answer line is set as a DEGREE SIGN, so the page reads [L1M(deg)T-2], [L1M(deg)T(deg)], [L(deg)M(deg)T1] - six occurrences. It is demonstrably a defect rather than a reading error on my part, because the subscript zero of v_0 two lines above and the zero exponent in Ex Q.3 (iii)'s own answer ([L0M1T-2I-1]) are both set as proper zeros. stem: The length, breadth and thickness of a rectangular sheet of metal are 4.234 m, 1.005 m, and 2.01 cm respectively. Give the area and volume of the sheet to correct significant figures.
_note: Book defect in the printed answer, and it is answer-affecting. The area 4.255 m^2 is correct (4.234 x 1.005 = 4.25517). The volume is NOT: the thickness is given as 2.01 CENTIMETRES = 0.0201 m, so the volume is 4.25517 x 0.0201 = 0.08553 m^3, i.e. 8.552 x 10^-2 m^3. The printed 8.552 m^3 is exactly what you get by multiplying 4.25517 by 2.01 as though the thickness were in metres, so the key has omitted the cm-to-m conversion and the answer is out by a factor of 100. The digits 8.552 are right; the magnitude is not. Second, and independent of the magnitude error: the question asks for the volume 'to correct significant figures', and the thickness 2.01 cm carries 3 significant figures, so the volume must be quoted to 3 (8.55 x 10^-2 m^3), not the 4 printed. Reached independently by two transcription passes.

stem: If the length of a cylinder is \(l = (4.00 \pm 0.001)\) cm, radius \(r = (0.0250 \pm 0.001)\) cm and mass \(m = (6.25 \pm 0.01)\) gm. Calculate the percentage error in the determination of density.
_note: Significant-figures inconsistency in the STEM, in a chapter whose subject is precision. The length is printed 4.00 +/- 0.001, where the value is quoted to 2 decimal places and the uncertainty to 3, i.e. finer than the value's own last digit; the radius is printed 0.0250 +/- 0.001, where the uncertainty is ten times COARSER than the value's last digit. The printed answer 8.185% follows exactly from the printed data (0.01/6.25 + 2 x 0.001/0.0250 + 0.001/4.00 = 0.08185) and is correct as an arithmetic result, but it is quoted to 4 significant figures against input uncertainties carrying 1. Transcribed as printed.
